### Step 2: Build one read-only status snapshot

# Durable Hook Integration and Truthful Status Design

## Context

GitHub issue #2264 reports that `entire status` can say checkpoints sync to a
remote even when Entire's Git hooks are absent. Related reports show a larger
failure mode: Lefthook can overwrite Entire-owned hook wrappers, checkpoint
capture then stops silently, and the user only learns about it by running a
diagnostic command. Two other status behaviors make the diagnosis harder:

- status describes the checkpoint sync destination without separately showing
  the effective checkpoint storage backend, so a project-level dedicated remote
  can appear to override a local `git-refs` choice even though the settings are
  orthogonal;
- status mutates dead-owner sessions while rendering and its JSON output
  deduplicates active sessions by agent, making sessions appear to disappear.

The work is ordered deliberately: make hook delivery durable first, surface a
failure at the point it occurs second, and then make status a faithful,
read-only view of the resulting state.

## Goals

1. Preserve Entire's Git lifecycle hooks when Lefthook refreshes its generated
   hooks.
2. Detect and report failed hook integration without requiring the user to run
   `entire status`.
3. Make `entire status` and `entire status --json` distinguish configured sync
   destination from operational sync health.
4. Show checkpoint storage and checkpoint sync as separate effective settings.
5. Show every active session and keep status read-only.

## Non-goals

- General integrations for every hook manager in this change. Existing native
  hook chaining remains the fallback for Husky, pre-commit, Overcommit, hk, and
  unknown managers.
- Editing or committing a repository's shared Lefthook configuration.
- Running `lefthook install` on the user's behalf.
- Changing checkpoint storage or remote selection semantics.
- Replacing the session sweeper or changing session expiry policy.
- Real-agent E2E tests.

## Design

### 1. Model the installed integration, not only hook-file ownership

Introduce a strategy-level Git hook integration health model. It records:

- mode: `native` or `lefthook`;
- state: `current`, `degraded`, `outdated`, `absent`, or `error`;
- manager, when applicable;
- a user-actionable reason when the state is not current.

`CheckGitHookIntegration` becomes the single read path used by setup, status,
doctor, and tests. Native mode retains the existing marker/content checks.
Lefthook mode verifies the clone-local configuration, all five Entire scripts,
and that the active hook path is either Lefthook-owned or a still-current
Entire wrapper that safely bridges to Lefthook during migration.

The five required hooks remain:

- `prepare-commit-msg`
- `commit-msg`
- `post-commit`
- `post-rewrite`
- `pre-push`

State semantics are explicit:

- `current`: all five hooks invoke Entire now and the selected owner will retain
  the integration when it refreshes;
- `degraded`: all five hooks invoke Entire now, but an overwriting manager is
  detected and durable manager integration is not verified;
- `outdated`: Entire-owned artifacts exist but their invocation contract cannot
  be verified, so current operation is not assumed;
- `absent`: one or more required invocation paths do not exist;
- `error`: health could not be inspected safely.

### 2. Install Entire as a clone-local Lefthook participant

Lefthook selection is deterministic. The detector separates non-local main
configs (`lefthook.*` / `.lefthook.*`) from local variants. Exactly one main
config selects Lefthook only when Lefthook is the sole detected manager capable
of overwriting Git hooks. Multiple main variants, a local-only configuration,
or coexistence with another overwriting manager is ambiguous: setup preserves a
working native integration, reports `degraded`, and asks the user to identify a
single owner. Non-overwriting managers may coexist. The only local file Entire
will create or merge is `lefthook-local.yml`; any other local variant alongside
the selected main config is a conflict and is left untouched.

When Lefthook is selected, `entire enable` and setup repair
install a clone-local integration rather than depending permanently on
Entire-owned files under `.git/hooks`:

- merge Entire-owned `scripts` entries into `lefthook-local.yml`;
- write one generated shell script per hook under
  `.lefthook-local/<hook>/entire.sh`;
- add the generated config and script directory to `.git/info/exclude` without
  disturbing existing patterns.

The script bodies preserve the current native-wrapper contract, including Git
arguments, `post-rewrite` stdin, and the non-swallowed `pre-push` result. Every
script emits a concise stderr warning when the `entire` binary is unavailable;
ordinary capture hooks retain their current fail-open behavior.

The merger owns only a clearly marked mapping entry per hook. It preserves
unrelated local configuration and comments. If another supported local
Lefthook file already exists, the YAML is invalid, or the Entire-owned entry
conflicts with a user-owned entry, installation stops with an actionable error
and leaves the existing native wrappers intact.

Installation is transactional at the operation level:

1. Snapshot files that may change.
2. Write scripts and merged local config through atomic replacement.
3. Re-read and verify the resulting integration.
4. If the current Entire wrappers chain saved Lefthook hooks, restore those
   saved hooks so Lefthook resumes ownership.
5. Re-check all five active hook paths.
6. On any error, restore the snapshots and return a typed integration error.

If there is no saved Lefthook hook to restore, the current Entire wrapper stays
in place. The clone-local Lefthook integration is already prepared, so a future
Lefthook install can replace the wrapper without dropping Entire. This avoids
requiring the Lefthook executable during migration and avoids a hookless window.

Repeated installation is idempotent. Linked worktrees are handled per worktree:
setup writes the local config in that worktree while Git hook ownership remains
resolved through the repository's effective hook path.

Uninstall is the inverse owned operation. `entire disable --uninstall` removes
only marked Entire script entries from `lefthook-local.yml`, deletes only
generated scripts whose ownership marker matches, and removes only Entire's
exact exclude patterns. It preserves unrelated YAML, comments, scripts, and
exclude rules. Native hook removal and Lefthook artifact removal share the same
snapshot/rollback mechanism; a partial failure makes uninstall fail non-zero and
remain safely retryable. Plain `entire disable` leaves integrations installed,
as it does today, so disabled hooks can exit silently and later be re-enabled.

### 3. Centralize repair and make failures visible immediately

All setup paths use `EnsureGitHookIntegration`; direct calls that install only
native wrappers are removed from enable, configure, and lifecycle repair.

Agent lifecycle behavior has two user-visible checkpoints:

- Session start performs a read-only health check and appends a warning to the
  normal agent banner when integration is unhealthy.
- Turn start attempts repair. If repair fails, it writes an agent-native hook
  response warning containing the failed mode and a concrete next action, while
  also recording operational detail in `.entire/logs/`.

Warnings are emitted at most once per session for the same health fingerprint,
then emitted again if the condition changes or a later repair fails differently.
The fingerprint is the stable tuple `(mode, state, manager, reason-code)` and is
stored as an optional field in the existing session state; free-form text is not
part of it. Session-start display naturally occurs once, while turn-start repair
consults and updates the persisted fingerprint.
This avoids warning on every prompt while ensuring the failure is visible in
the workflow that depends on hooks. Direct Git users receive the generated
script's stderr warning when the binary cannot execute. A completely removed
hook cannot warn on its own, so agent lifecycle checks and `doctor` remain the
repair paths for that case.

Hook protocol output must use each agent's existing `HookResponseWriter`; raw
stdout is not used. Logs contain IDs, paths, manager, and state only—never user
prompts, file content, or commit messages.

### 4. Make status describe operational truth

Both text and JSON status consume one health snapshot so they cannot disagree.
When integration is current, status reports the configured checkpoint sync
destination as it does today. Degraded integration is reported as working now
but vulnerable to manager refresh. Outdated, absent, or error states report sync
as blocked and include the hook reason; status never presents a configured
remote as an active promise when current operation is not verified.

JSON retains the existing checkpoint remote/source keys for compatibility and
adds:

- `checkpoint_sync_state`: `ready`, `degraded`, or `blocked`;
- `git_hooks`: mode, state, manager, and optional reason.

The mapping is fixed: hook `current` -> sync `ready`; hook `degraded` -> sync
`degraded`; hook `outdated`, `absent`, or `error` -> sync `blocked`.

Issue #2264 is satisfied when absent hooks produce a blocked text line and a
blocked JSON state even if a checkpoint remote is configured.

### 5. Separate checkpoint storage from sync destination

Status loads the effective checkpoint backend through
`settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig`, which already applies the supported local
checkpoint override behavior. It displays two concepts independently:

- storage: for example, Git refs;
- sync destination: for example, a dedicated GitHub checkpoint repository.

The existing remote/source JSON keys remain. JSON adds
`checkpoint_storage_backend`. A project-level `checkpoint_remote` and a local
`git-refs` backend are both shown because they do not override one another.

### 6. Make session reporting complete and read-only

Status stops calling `finalizeExitedSessions`. Dead-owner cleanup remains the
responsibility of the existing session sweep and explicit doctor/cleanup paths.
Status may label a dead-owner session `exited`, but rendering never changes its
phase, condenses its files, or writes state.

Text and JSON share the same active-session collection and deterministic sort.
JSON no longer deduplicates by agent; each session is represented independently.
Existing fields remain and entries add the identity required to distinguish
same-agent sessions:

- session ID;
- worktree ID and path;
- branch;
- started and last-active timestamps when available.

Adding fields is backward compatible for consumers that read the existing
subset. Returning multiple same-agent entries is the intended correction to the
status contract.

A session whose persisted phase is active or idle remains in `active_sessions`
until the dedicated sweeper persists an ended phase, even when its owner is
known dead. Status derives and displays `exited` for that entry without writing.
Sessions sort by last-active time descending, then session ID ascending as the
stable tie-breaker.

## Failure handling

- Unsupported or ambiguous Lefthook ownership/configuration: preserve a working
  native integration, classify it degraded, warn in the active agent, and give
  a concrete manual remediation path. If no working native path exists, report
  error/blocked.
- Partial filesystem failure: roll back every file captured by the transaction;
  if rollback itself fails, report both errors and mark health `error`.
- Lefthook later overwrites `.git/hooks`: clone-local scripts remain configured,
  so Entire continues to run through Lefthook.
- Generated script cannot locate `entire`: warn on stderr. `pre-push` retains
  its blocking semantics; other capture hooks fail open as today.
- Health inspection error: status reports blocked/unknown health and preserves
  configured destination details for diagnosis.

## Test strategy

Unit tests cover health classification, YAML merge preservation/conflicts,
script argument and stdin contracts, idempotence, rollback, effective settings,
and full session serialization. Git-touching tests use isolated temporary
repositories.

Integration tests simulate:

1. Lefthook installed before Entire enable.
2. Entire enabled before Lefthook overwrites all hook files.
3. Repeated lifecycle repair.
4. A failed repair surfacing through an agent-native response.
5. Issue #2264 in text and JSON.
6. Multiple active sessions from the same agent remaining visible.

# Durable Hook Integration and Truthful Status Design

## Context

GitHub issue #2264 reports that `entire status` can say checkpoints sync to a
remote even when Entire's Git hooks are absent. Related reports show a larger
failure mode: Lefthook can overwrite Entire-owned hook wrappers, checkpoint
capture then stops silently, and the user only learns about it by running a
diagnostic command. Two other status behaviors make the diagnosis harder:

- status describes the checkpoint sync destination without separately showing
  the effective checkpoint storage backend, so a project-level dedicated remote
  can appear to override a local `git-refs` choice even though the settings are
  orthogonal;
- status mutates dead-owner sessions while rendering and its JSON output
  deduplicates active sessions by agent, making sessions appear to disappear.

The work is ordered deliberately: make hook delivery durable first, surface a
failure at the point it occurs second, and then make status a faithful,
read-only view of the resulting state.

## Goals

1. Preserve Entire's Git lifecycle hooks when Lefthook refreshes its generated
   hooks.
2. Detect and report failed hook integration without requiring the user to run
   `entire status`.
3. Make `entire status` and `entire status --json` distinguish configured sync
   destination from operational sync health.
4. Show checkpoint storage and checkpoint sync as separate effective settings.
5. Show every active session and keep status read-only.

## Non-goals

- General integrations for every hook manager in this change. Existing native
  hook chaining remains the fallback for Husky, pre-commit, Overcommit, hk, and
  unknown managers.
- Editing or committing a repository's shared Lefthook configuration.
- Running `lefthook install` on the user's behalf.
- Changing checkpoint storage or remote selection semantics.
- Replacing the session sweeper or changing session expiry policy.
- Real-agent E2E tests.

## Design

### 1. Model the installed integration, not only hook-file ownership

Introduce a strategy-level Git hook integration health model. It records:

- mode: `native` or `lefthook`;
- state: `current`, `degraded`, `outdated`, `absent`, or `error`;
- manager, when applicable;
- a user-actionable reason when the state is not current.

`CheckGitHookIntegration` becomes the single read path used by setup, status,
doctor, and tests. Native mode retains the existing marker/content checks.
Lefthook mode verifies the clone-local configuration, all five Entire scripts,
and that the active hook path is either Lefthook-owned or a still-current
Entire wrapper that safely bridges to Lefthook during migration.

The five required hooks remain:

- `prepare-commit-msg`
- `commit-msg`
- `post-commit`
- `post-rewrite`
- `pre-push`

State semantics are explicit:

- `current`: all five hooks invoke Entire now and the selected owner will retain
  the integration when it refreshes;
- `degraded`: all five hooks invoke Entire now, but an overwriting manager is
  detected and durable manager integration is not verified;
- `outdated`: Entire-owned artifacts exist but their invocation contract cannot
  be verified, so current operation is not assumed;
- `absent`: one or more required invocation paths do not exist;
- `error`: health could not be inspected safely.

### 2. Install Entire as a clone-local Lefthook participant

Lefthook selection is deterministic. The detector separates non-local main
configs (`lefthook.*` / `.lefthook.*`) from local variants. Exactly one main
config selects Lefthook only when Lefthook is the sole detected manager capable
of overwriting Git hooks. Multiple main variants, a local-only configuration,
or coexistence with another overwriting manager is ambiguous: setup preserves a
working native integration, reports `degraded`, and asks the user to identify a
single owner. Non-overwriting managers may coexist. The only local file Entire
will create or merge is `lefthook-local.yml`; any other local variant alongside
the selected main config is a conflict and is left untouched.

When Lefthook is selected, `entire enable` and setup repair
install a clone-local integration rather than depending permanently on
Entire-owned files under `.git/hooks`:

- merge Entire-owned `scripts` entries into `lefthook-local.yml`;
- write one generated shell script per hook under
  `.lefthook-local/<hook>/entire.sh`;
- add the generated config and script directory to `.git/info/exclude` without
  disturbing existing patterns.

The script bodies preserve the current native-wrapper contract, including Git
arguments, `post-rewrite` stdin, and the non-swallowed `pre-push` result. Every
script emits a concise stderr warning when the `entire` binary is unavailable;
ordinary capture hooks retain their current fail-open behavior.

The merger owns only a clearly marked mapping entry per hook. It preserves
unrelated local configuration and comments. If another supported local
Lefthook file already exists, the YAML is invalid, or the Entire-owned entry
conflicts with a user-owned entry, installation stops with an actionable error
and leaves the existing native wrappers intact.

Installation is transactional at the operation level:

1. Snapshot files that may change.
2. Write scripts and merged local config through atomic replacement.
3. Re-read and verify the resulting integration.
4. If the current Entire wrappers chain saved Lefthook hooks, restore those
   saved hooks so Lefthook resumes ownership.
5. Re-check all five active hook paths.
6. On any error, restore the snapshots and return a typed integration error.

If there is no saved Lefthook hook to restore, the current Entire wrapper stays
in place. The clone-local Lefthook integration is already prepared, so a future
Lefthook install can replace the wrapper without dropping Entire. This avoids
requiring the Lefthook executable during migration and avoids a hookless window.

Repeated installation is idempotent. Linked worktrees are handled per worktree:
setup writes the local config in that worktree while Git hook ownership remains
resolved through the repository's effective hook path.

Uninstall is the inverse owned operation. `entire disable --uninstall` removes
only marked Entire script entries from `lefthook-local.yml`, deletes only
generated scripts whose ownership marker matches, and removes only Entire's
exact exclude patterns. It preserves unrelated YAML, comments, scripts, and
exclude rules. Native hook removal and Lefthook artifact removal share the same
snapshot/rollback mechanism; a partial failure makes uninstall fail non-zero and
remain safely retryable. Plain `entire disable` leaves integrations installed,
as it does today, so disabled hooks can exit silently and later be re-enabled.

### 3. Centralize repair and make failures visible immediately

All setup paths use `EnsureGitHookIntegration`; direct calls that install only
native wrappers are removed from enable, configure, and lifecycle repair.

Agent lifecycle behavior has two user-visible checkpoints:

- Session start performs a read-only health check and appends a warning to the
  normal agent banner when integration is unhealthy.
- Turn start attempts repair. If repair fails, it writes an agent-native hook
  response warning containing the failed mode and a concrete next action, while
  also recording operational detail in `.entire/logs/`.

Warnings are emitted at most once per session for the same health fingerprint,
then emitted again if the condition changes or a later repair fails differently.
The fingerprint is the stable tuple `(mode, state, manager, reason-code)` and is
stored as an optional field in the existing session state; free-form text is not
part of it. Session-start display naturally occurs once, while turn-start repair
consults and updates the persisted fingerprint.
This avoids warning on every prompt while ensuring the failure is visible in
the workflow that depends on hooks. Direct Git users receive the generated
script's stderr warning when the binary cannot execute. A completely removed
hook cannot warn on its own, so agent lifecycle checks and `doctor` remain the
repair paths for that case.

Hook protocol output must use each agent's existing `HookResponseWriter`; raw
stdout is not used. Logs contain IDs, paths, manager, and state only—never user
prompts, file content, or commit messages.

### 4. Make status describe operational truth

Both text and JSON status consume one health snapshot so they cannot disagree.
When integration is current, status reports the configured checkpoint sync
destination as it does today. Degraded integration is reported as working now
but vulnerable to manager refresh. Outdated, absent, or error states report sync
as blocked and include the hook reason; status never presents a configured
remote as an active promise when current operation is not verified.

JSON retains the existing checkpoint remote/source keys for compatibility and
adds:

- `checkpoint_sync_state`: `ready`, `degraded`, or `blocked`;
- `git_hooks`: mode, state, manager, and optional reason.

The mapping is fixed: hook `current` -> sync `ready`; hook `degraded` -> sync
`degraded`; hook `outdated`, `absent`, or `error` -> sync `blocked`.

Issue #2264 is satisfied when absent hooks produce a blocked text line and a
blocked JSON state even if a checkpoint remote is configured.

### 5. Separate checkpoint storage from sync destination

Status loads the effective checkpoint backend through
`settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig`, which already applies the supported local
checkpoint override behavior. It displays two concepts independently:

- storage: for example, Git refs;
- sync destination: for example, a dedicated GitHub checkpoint repository.

The existing remote/source JSON keys remain. JSON adds
`checkpoint_storage_backend`. A project-level `checkpoint_remote` and a local
`git-refs` backend are both shown because they do not override one another.

### 6. Make session reporting complete and read-only

Status stops calling `finalizeExitedSessions`. Dead-owner cleanup remains the
responsibility of the existing session sweep and explicit doctor/cleanup paths.
Status may label a dead-owner session `exited`, but rendering never changes its
phase, condenses its files, or writes state.

Text and JSON share the same active-session collection and deterministic sort.
JSON no longer deduplicates by agent; each session is represented independently.
Existing fields remain and entries add the identity required to distinguish
same-agent sessions:

- session ID;
- worktree ID and path;
- branch;
- started and last-active timestamps when available.

Adding fields is backward compatible for consumers that read the existing
subset. Returning multiple same-agent entries is the intended correction to the
status contract.

A session whose persisted phase is active or idle remains in `active_sessions`
until the dedicated sweeper persists an ended phase, even when its owner is
known dead. Status derives and displays `exited` for that entry without writing.
Sessions sort by last-active time descending, then session ID ascending as the
stable tie-breaker.

## Failure handling

- Unsupported or ambiguous Lefthook ownership/configuration: preserve a working
  native integration, classify it degraded, warn in the active agent, and give
  a concrete manual remediation path. If no working native path exists, report
  error/blocked.
- Partial filesystem failure: roll back every file captured by the transaction;
  if rollback itself fails, report both errors and mark health `error`.
- Lefthook later overwrites `.git/hooks`: clone-local scripts remain configured,
  so Entire continues to run through Lefthook.
- Generated script cannot locate `entire`: warn on stderr. `pre-push` retains
  its blocking semantics; other capture hooks fail open as today.
- Health inspection error: status reports blocked/unknown health and preserves
  configured destination details for diagnosis.

## Test strategy

Unit tests cover health classification, YAML merge preservation/conflicts,
script argument and stdin contracts, idempotence, rollback, effective settings,
and full session serialization. Git-touching tests use isolated temporary
repositories.

Integration tests simulate:

1. Lefthook installed before Entire enable.
2. Entire enabled before Lefthook overwrites all hook files.
3. Repeated lifecycle repair.
4. A failed repair surfacing through an agent-native response.
5. Issue #2264 in text and JSON.
6. Multiple active sessions from the same agent remaining visible.

# Durable Hook Integration and Truthful Status Design

## Context

GitHub issue #2264 reports that `entire status` can say checkpoints sync to a
remote even when Entire's Git hooks are absent. Related reports show a larger
failure mode: Lefthook can overwrite Entire-owned hook wrappers, checkpoint
capture then stops silently, and the user only learns about it by running a
diagnostic command. Two other status behaviors make the diagnosis harder:

- status describes the checkpoint sync destination without separately showing
  the effective checkpoint storage backend, so a project-level dedicated remote
  can appear to override a local `git-refs` choice even though the settings are
  orthogonal;
- status mutates dead-owner sessions while rendering and its JSON output
  deduplicates active sessions by agent, making sessions appear to disappear.

The work is ordered deliberately: make hook delivery durable first, surface a
failure at the point it occurs second, and then make status a faithful,
read-only view of the resulting state.

## Goals

1. Preserve Entire's Git lifecycle hooks when Lefthook refreshes its generated
   hooks.
2. Detect and report failed hook integration without requiring the user to run
   `entire status`.
3. Make `entire status` and `entire status --json` distinguish configured sync
   destination from operational sync health.
4. Show checkpoint storage and checkpoint sync as separate effective settings.
5. Show every active session and keep status read-only.

## Non-goals

- General integrations for every hook manager in this change. Existing native
  hook chaining remains the fallback for Husky, pre-commit, Overcommit, hk, and
  unknown managers.
- Editing or committing a repository's shared Lefthook configuration.
- Running `lefthook install` on the user's behalf.
- Changing checkpoint storage or remote selection semantics.
- Replacing the session sweeper or changing session expiry policy.
- Real-agent E2E tests.

## Design

### 1. Model the installed integration, not only hook-file ownership

Introduce a strategy-level Git hook integration health model. It records:

- mode: `native` or `lefthook`;
- state: `current`, `degraded`, `outdated`, `absent`, or `error`;
- manager, when applicable;
- a user-actionable reason when the state is not current.

`CheckGitHookIntegration` becomes the single read path used by setup, status,
doctor, and tests. Native mode retains the existing marker/content checks.
Lefthook mode verifies the clone-local configuration, all five Entire scripts,
and that the active hook path is either Lefthook-owned or a still-current
Entire wrapper that safely bridges to Lefthook during migration.

The five required hooks remain:

- `prepare-commit-msg`
- `commit-msg`
- `post-commit`
- `post-rewrite`
- `pre-push`

State semantics are explicit:

- `current`: all five hooks invoke Entire now and the selected owner will retain
  the integration when it refreshes;
- `degraded`: all five hooks invoke Entire now, but an overwriting manager is
  detected and durable manager integration is not verified;
- `outdated`: Entire-owned artifacts exist but their invocation contract cannot
  be verified, so current operation is not assumed;
- `absent`: one or more required invocation paths do not exist;
- `error`: health could not be inspected safely.

### 2. Install Entire as a clone-local Lefthook participant

Lefthook selection is deterministic. The detector separates non-local main
configs (`lefthook.*` / `.lefthook.*`) from local variants. Exactly one main
config selects Lefthook only when Lefthook is the sole detected manager capable
of overwriting Git hooks. Multiple main variants, a local-only configuration,
or coexistence with another overwriting manager is ambiguous: setup preserves a
working native integration, reports `degraded`, and asks the user to identify a
single owner. Non-overwriting managers may coexist. The only local file Entire
will create or merge is `lefthook-local.yml`; any other local variant alongside
the selected main config is a conflict and is left untouched.

When Lefthook is selected, `entire enable` and setup repair
install a clone-local integration rather than depending permanently on
Entire-owned files under `.git/hooks`:

- merge Entire-owned `scripts` entries into `lefthook-local.yml`;
- write one generated shell script per hook under
  `.lefthook-local/<hook>/entire.sh`;
- add the generated config and script directory to `.git/info/exclude` without
  disturbing existing patterns.

The script bodies preserve the current native-wrapper contract, including Git
arguments, `post-rewrite` stdin, and the non-swallowed `pre-push` result. Every
script emits a concise stderr warning when the `entire` binary is unavailable;
ordinary capture hooks retain their current fail-open behavior.

The merger owns only a clearly marked mapping entry per hook. It preserves
unrelated local configuration and comments. If another supported local
Lefthook file already exists, the YAML is invalid, or the Entire-owned entry
conflicts with a user-owned entry, installation stops with an actionable error
and leaves the existing native wrappers intact.

Installation is transactional at the operation level:

1. Snapshot files that may change.
2. Write scripts and merged local config through atomic replacement.
3. Re-read and verify the resulting integration.
4. If the current Entire wrappers chain saved Lefthook hooks, restore those
   saved hooks so Lefthook resumes ownership.
5. Re-check all five active hook paths.
6. On any error, restore the snapshots and return a typed integration error.

If there is no saved Lefthook hook to restore, the current Entire wrapper stays
in place. The clone-local Lefthook integration is already prepared, so a future
Lefthook install can replace the wrapper without dropping Entire. This avoids
requiring the Lefthook executable during migration and avoids a hookless window.

Repeated installation is idempotent. Linked worktrees are handled per worktree:
setup writes the local config in that worktree while Git hook ownership remains
resolved through the repository's effective hook path.

Uninstall is the inverse owned operation. `entire disable --uninstall` removes
only marked Entire script entries from `lefthook-local.yml`, deletes only
generated scripts whose ownership marker matches, and removes only Entire's
exact exclude patterns. It preserves unrelated YAML, comments, scripts, and
exclude rules. Native hook removal and Lefthook artifact removal share the same
snapshot/rollback mechanism; a partial failure makes uninstall fail non-zero and
remain safely retryable. Plain `entire disable` leaves integrations installed,
as it does today, so disabled hooks can exit silently and later be re-enabled.

### 3. Centralize repair and make failures visible immediately

All setup paths use `EnsureGitHookIntegration`; direct calls that install only
native wrappers are removed from enable, configure, and lifecycle repair.

Agent lifecycle behavior has two user-visible checkpoints:

- Session start performs a read-only health check and appends a warning to the
  normal agent banner when integration is unhealthy.
- Turn start attempts repair. If repair fails, it writes an agent-native hook
  response warning containing the failed mode and a concrete next action, while
  also recording operational detail in `.entire/logs/`.

Warnings are emitted at most once per session for the same health fingerprint,
then emitted again if the condition changes or a later repair fails differently.
The fingerprint is the stable tuple `(mode, state, manager, reason-code)` and is
stored as an optional field in the existing session state; free-form text is not
part of it. Session-start display naturally occurs once, while turn-start repair
consults and updates the persisted fingerprint.
This avoids warning on every prompt while ensuring the failure is visible in
the workflow that depends on hooks. Direct Git users receive the generated
script's stderr warning when the binary cannot execute. A completely removed
hook cannot warn on its own, so agent lifecycle checks and `doctor` remain the
repair paths for that case.

Hook protocol output must use each agent's existing `HookResponseWriter`; raw
stdout is not used. Logs contain IDs, paths, manager, and state only—never user
prompts, file content, or commit messages.

### 4. Make status describe operational truth

Both text and JSON status consume one health snapshot so they cannot disagree.
When integration is current, status reports the configured checkpoint sync
destination as it does today. Degraded integration is reported as working now
but vulnerable to manager refresh. Outdated, absent, or error states report sync
as blocked and include the hook reason; status never presents a configured
remote as an active promise when current operation is not verified.

JSON retains the existing checkpoint remote/source keys for compatibility and
adds:

- `checkpoint_sync_state`: `ready`, `degraded`, or `blocked`;
- `git_hooks`: mode, state, manager, and optional reason.

The mapping is fixed: hook `current` -> sync `ready`; hook `degraded` -> sync
`degraded`; hook `outdated`, `absent`, or `error` -> sync `blocked`.

Issue #2264 is satisfied when absent hooks produce a blocked text line and a
blocked JSON state even if a checkpoint remote is configured.

### 5. Separate checkpoint storage from sync destination

Status loads the effective checkpoint backend through
`settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig`, which already applies the supported local
checkpoint override behavior. It displays two concepts independently:

- storage: for example, Git refs;
- sync destination: for example, a dedicated GitHub checkpoint repository.

The existing remote/source JSON keys remain. JSON adds
`checkpoint_storage_backend`. A project-level `checkpoint_remote` and a local
`git-refs` backend are both shown because they do not override one another.

### 6. Make session reporting complete and read-only

Status stops calling `finalizeExitedSessions`. Dead-owner cleanup remains the
responsibility of the existing session sweep and explicit doctor/cleanup paths.
Status may label a dead-owner session `exited`, but rendering never changes its
phase, condenses its files, or writes state.

Text and JSON share the same active-session collection and deterministic sort.
JSON no longer deduplicates by agent; each session is represented independently.
Existing fields remain and entries add the identity required to distinguish
same-agent sessions:

- session ID;
- worktree ID and path;
- branch;
- started and last-active timestamps when available.

Adding fields is backward compatible for consumers that read the existing
subset. Returning multiple same-agent entries is the intended correction to the
status contract.

A session whose persisted phase is active or idle remains in `active_sessions`
until the dedicated sweeper persists an ended phase, even when its owner is
known dead. Status derives and displays `exited` for that entry without writing.
Sessions sort by last-active time descending, then session ID ascending as the
stable tie-breaker.

## Failure handling

- Unsupported or ambiguous Lefthook ownership/configuration: preserve a working
  native integration, classify it degraded, warn in the active agent, and give
  a concrete manual remediation path. If no working native path exists, report
  error/blocked.
- Partial filesystem failure: roll back every file captured by the transaction;
  if rollback itself fails, report both errors and mark health `error`.
- Lefthook later overwrites `.git/hooks`: clone-local scripts remain configured,
  so Entire continues to run through Lefthook.
- Generated script cannot locate `entire`: warn on stderr. `pre-push` retains
  its blocking semantics; other capture hooks fail open as today.
- Health inspection error: status reports blocked/unknown health and preserves
  configured destination details for diagnosis.

## Test strategy

Unit tests cover health classification, YAML merge preservation/conflicts,
script argument and stdin contracts, idempotence, rollback, effective settings,
and full session serialization. Git-touching tests use isolated temporary
repositories.

Integration tests simulate:

1. Lefthook installed before Entire enable.
2. Entire enabled before Lefthook overwrites all hook files.
3. Repeated lifecycle repair.
4. A failed repair surfacing through an agent-native response.
5. Issue #2264 in text and JSON.
6. Multiple active sessions from the same agent remaining visible.

# Durable Hook Integration and Truthful Status Design

## Context

GitHub issue #2264 reports that `entire status` can say checkpoints sync to a
remote even when Entire's Git hooks are absent. Related reports show a larger
failure mode: Lefthook can overwrite Entire-owned hook wrappers, checkpoint
capture then stops silently, and the user only learns about it by running a
diagnostic command. Two other status behaviors make the diagnosis harder:

- status describes the checkpoint sync destination without separately showing
  the effective checkpoint storage backend, so a project-level dedicated remote
  can appear to override a local `git-refs` choice even though the settings are
  orthogonal;
- status mutates dead-owner sessions while rendering and its JSON output
  deduplicates active sessions by agent, making sessions appear to disappear.

The work is ordered deliberately: make hook delivery durable first, surface a
failure at the point it occurs second, and then make status a faithful,
read-only view of the resulting state.

## Goals

1. Preserve Entire's Git lifecycle hooks when Lefthook refreshes its generated
   hooks.
2. Detect and report failed hook integration without requiring the user to run
   `entire status`.
3. Make `entire status` and `entire status --json` distinguish configured sync
   destination from operational sync health.
4. Show checkpoint storage and checkpoint sync as separate effective settings.
5. Show every active session and keep status read-only.

## Non-goals

- General integrations for every hook manager in this change. Existing native
  hook chaining remains the fallback for Husky, pre-commit, Overcommit, hk, and
  unknown managers.
- Editing or committing a repository's shared Lefthook configuration.
- Running `lefthook install` on the user's behalf.
- Changing checkpoint storage or remote selection semantics.
- Replacing the session sweeper or changing session expiry policy.
- Real-agent E2E tests.

## Design

### 1. Model the installed integration, not only hook-file ownership

Introduce a strategy-level Git hook integration health model. It records:

- mode: `native` or `lefthook`;
- state: `current`, `degraded`, `outdated`, `absent`, or `error`;
- manager, when applicable;
- a user-actionable reason when the state is not current.

`CheckGitHookIntegration` becomes the single read path used by setup, status,
doctor, and tests. Native mode retains the existing marker/content checks.
Lefthook mode verifies the clone-local configuration, all five Entire scripts,
and that the active hook path is either Lefthook-owned or a still-current
Entire wrapper that safely bridges to Lefthook during migration.

The five required hooks remain:

- `prepare-commit-msg`
- `commit-msg`
- `post-commit`
- `post-rewrite`
- `pre-push`

State semantics are explicit:

- `current`: all five hooks invoke Entire now and the selected owner will retain
  the integration when it refreshes;
- `degraded`: all five hooks invoke Entire now, but an overwriting manager is
  detected and durable manager integration is not verified;
- `outdated`: Entire-owned artifacts exist but their invocation contract cannot
  be verified, so current operation is not assumed;
- `absent`: one or more required invocation paths do not exist;
- `error`: health could not be inspected safely.

### 2. Install Entire as a clone-local Lefthook participant

Lefthook selection is deterministic. The detector separates non-local main
configs (`lefthook.*` / `.lefthook.*`) from local variants. Exactly one main
config selects Lefthook only when Lefthook is the sole detected manager capable
of overwriting Git hooks. Multiple main variants, a local-only configuration,
or coexistence with another overwriting manager is ambiguous: setup preserves a
working native integration, reports `degraded`, and asks the user to identify a
single owner. Non-overwriting managers may coexist. The only local file Entire
will create or merge is `lefthook-local.yml`; any other local variant alongside
the selected main config is a conflict and is left untouched.

When Lefthook is selected, `entire enable` and setup repair
install a clone-local integration rather than depending permanently on
Entire-owned files under `.git/hooks`:

- merge Entire-owned `scripts` entries into `lefthook-local.yml`;
- write one generated shell script per hook under
  `.lefthook-local/<hook>/entire.sh`;
- add the generated config and script directory to `.git/info/exclude` without
  disturbing existing patterns.

The script bodies preserve the current native-wrapper contract, including Git
arguments, `post-rewrite` stdin, and the non-swallowed `pre-push` result. Every
script emits a concise stderr warning when the `entire` binary is unavailable;
ordinary capture hooks retain their current fail-open behavior.

The merger owns only a clearly marked mapping entry per hook. It preserves
unrelated local configuration and comments. If another supported local
Lefthook file already exists, the YAML is invalid, or the Entire-owned entry
conflicts with a user-owned entry, installation stops with an actionable error
and leaves the existing native wrappers intact.

Installation is transactional at the operation level:

1. Snapshot files that may change.
2. Write scripts and merged local config through atomic replacement.
3. Re-read and verify the resulting integration.
4. If the current Entire wrappers chain saved Lefthook hooks, restore those
   saved hooks so Lefthook resumes ownership.
5. Re-check all five active hook paths.
6. On any error, restore the snapshots and return a typed integration error.

If there is no saved Lefthook hook to restore, the current Entire wrapper stays
in place. The clone-local Lefthook integration is already prepared, so a future
Lefthook install can replace the wrapper without dropping Entire. This avoids
requiring the Lefthook executable during migration and avoids a hookless window.

Repeated installation is idempotent. Linked worktrees are handled per worktree:
setup writes the local config in that worktree while Git hook ownership remains
resolved through the repository's effective hook path.

Uninstall is the inverse owned operation. `entire disable --uninstall` removes
only marked Entire script entries from `lefthook-local.yml`, deletes only
generated scripts whose ownership marker matches, and removes only Entire's
exact exclude patterns. It preserves unrelated YAML, comments, scripts, and
exclude rules. Native hook removal and Lefthook artifact removal share the same
snapshot/rollback mechanism; a partial failure makes uninstall fail non-zero and
remain safely retryable. Plain `entire disable` leaves integrations installed,
as it does today, so disabled hooks can exit silently and later be re-enabled.

### 3. Centralize repair and make failures visible immediately

All setup paths use `EnsureGitHookIntegration`; direct calls that install only
native wrappers are removed from enable, configure, and lifecycle repair.

Agent lifecycle behavior has two user-visible checkpoints:

- Session start performs a read-only health check and appends a warning to the
  normal agent banner when integration is unhealthy.
- Turn start attempts repair. If repair fails, it writes an agent-native hook
  response warning containing the failed mode and a concrete next action, while
  also recording operational detail in `.entire/logs/`.

Warnings are emitted at most once per session for the same health fingerprint,
then emitted again if the condition changes or a later repair fails differently.
The fingerprint is the stable tuple `(mode, state, manager, reason-code)` and is
stored as an optional field in the existing session state; free-form text is not
part of it. Session-start display naturally occurs once, while turn-start repair
consults and updates the persisted fingerprint.
This avoids warning on every prompt while ensuring the failure is visible in
the workflow that depends on hooks. Direct Git users receive the generated
script's stderr warning when the binary cannot execute. A completely removed
hook cannot warn on its own, so agent lifecycle checks and `doctor` remain the
repair paths for that case.

Hook protocol output must use each agent's existing `HookResponseWriter`; raw
stdout is not used. Logs contain IDs, paths, manager, and state only—never user
prompts, file content, or commit messages.

### 4. Make status describe operational truth

Both text and JSON status consume one health snapshot so they cannot disagree.
When integration is current, status reports the configured checkpoint sync
destination as it does today. Degraded integration is reported as working now
but vulnerable to manager refresh. Outdated, absent, or error states report sync
as blocked and include the hook reason; status never presents a configured
remote as an active promise when current operation is not verified.

JSON retains the existing checkpoint remote/source keys for compatibility and
adds:

- `checkpoint_sync_state`: `ready`, `degraded`, or `blocked`;
- `git_hooks`: mode, state, manager, and optional reason.

The mapping is fixed: hook `current` -> sync `ready`; hook `degraded` -> sync
`degraded`; hook `outdated`, `absent`, or `error` -> sync `blocked`.

Issue #2264 is satisfied when absent hooks produce a blocked text line and a
blocked JSON state even if a checkpoint remote is configured.

### 5. Separate checkpoint storage from sync destination

Status loads the effective checkpoint backend through
`settings.LoadCheckpointsConfig`, which already applies the supported local
checkpoint override behavior. It displays two concepts independently:

- storage: for example, Git refs;
- sync destination: for example, a dedicated GitHub checkpoint repository.

The existing remote/source JSON keys remain. JSON adds
`checkpoint_storage_backend`. A project-level `checkpoint_remote` and a local
`git-refs` backend are both shown because they do not override one another.

### 6. Make session reporting complete and read-only

Status stops calling `finalizeExitedSessions`. Dead-owner cleanup remains the
responsibility of the existing session sweep and explicit doctor/cleanup paths.
Status may label a dead-owner session `exited`, but rendering never changes its
phase, condenses its files, or writes state.

Text and JSON share the same active-session collection and deterministic sort.
JSON no longer deduplicates by agent; each session is represented independently.
Existing fields remain and entries add the identity required to distinguish
same-agent sessions:

- session ID;
- worktree ID and path;
- branch;
- started and last-active timestamps when available.

Adding fields is backward compatible for consumers that read the existing
subset. Returning multiple same-agent entries is the intended correction to the
status contract.

A session whose persisted phase is active or idle remains in `active_sessions`
until the dedicated sweeper persists an ended phase, even when its owner is
known dead. Status derives and displays `exited` for that entry without writing.
Sessions sort by last-active time descending, then session ID ascending as the
stable tie-breaker.

## Failure handling

- Unsupported or ambiguous Lefthook ownership/configuration: preserve a working
  native integration, classify it degraded, warn in the active agent, and give
  a concrete manual remediation path. If no working native path exists, report
  error/blocked.
- Partial filesystem failure: roll back every file captured by the transaction;
  if rollback itself fails, report both errors and mark health `error`.
- Lefthook later overwrites `.git/hooks`: clone-local scripts remain configured,
  so Entire continues to run through Lefthook.
- Generated script cannot locate `entire`: warn on stderr. `pre-push` retains
  its blocking semantics; other capture hooks fail open as today.
- Health inspection error: status reports blocked/unknown health and preserves
  configured destination details for diagnosis.

## Test strategy

Unit tests cover health classification, YAML merge preservation/conflicts,
script argument and stdin contracts, idempotence, rollback, effective settings,
and full session serialization. Git-touching tests use isolated temporary
repositories.

Integration tests simulate:

1. Lefthook installed before Entire enable.
2. Entire enabled before Lefthook overwrites all hook files.
3. Repeated lifecycle repair.
4. A failed repair surfacing through an agent-native response.
5. Issue #2264 in text and JSON.
6. Multiple active sessions from the same agent remaining visible.

const patch = "*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /Users/peytonmontei/Documents/Documents - Peyton’s MacBook Pro/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/support/e2e/tests/lefthook_durable_test.go
+//go:build e2e
+
+package tests
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"encoding/json"
+	"fmt"
+	"os"
+	"path/filepath"
+	"testing"
+	"time"
+
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/execx"
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/e2e/entire"
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/e2e/testutil"
+	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
+)
+
+// TestLefthookRefreshKeepsAgentCommitCheckpointed exercises the user-visible
+// failure from issue #2264 end to end: Lefthook takes ownership of every live
+// Git hook after Entire was enabled, but the next real agent commit must still
+// be captured without requiring the user to run `entire status` first.
+func TestLefthookRefreshKeepsAgentCommitCheckpointed(t *testing.T) {
+	testutil.ForEachAgent(t, 3*time.Minute, func(t *testing.T, s *testutil.RepoState, ctx context.Context) {
+		lefthookConfig := filepath.Join(s.Dir, "lefthook.yml")
+		require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(lefthookConfig, []byte("pre-commit: {}\n"), 0o644))
+		s.Git(t, "add", "lefthook.yml")
+		s.Git(t, "commit", "-m", "Configure Lefthook")
+
+		// Re-enable after Lefthook appears so Entire creates its clone-local
+		// configuration and generated scripts while native hooks still bridge
+		// the transition.
+		entire.Enable(t, s.Dir, s.Agent.EntireAgent())
+
+		hooksDir := testutil.GitOutput(t, s.Dir, "rev-parse", "--git-path", "hooks")
+		if !filepath.IsAbs(hooksDir) {
+			hooksDir = filepath.Join(s.Dir, hooksDir)
+		}
+		for _, hook := range []string{"prepare-commit-msg", "commit-msg", "post-commit", "post-rewrite", "pre-push"} {
+			require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(
+				filepath.Join(hooksDir, hook),
+				[]byte(simulatedLefthookLauncher(hook)),
+				0o755,
+			))
+		}
+
+		// Status is only an assertion here, not the repair trigger: the launchers
+		// have already replaced Entire's native wrappers.
+		statusCmd := execx.NonInteractive(ctx, entire.BinPath(), "status", "--json")
+		statusCmd.Dir = s.Dir
+		statusOut, err := statusCmd.CombinedOutput()
+		require.NoError(t, err, "entire status --json failed: %s", statusOut)
+		var status struct {
+			CheckpointSyncState string `json:"checkpoint_sync_state"`
+			GitHooks            struct {
+				Mode  string `json:"mode"`
+				State string `json:"state"`
+			} `json:"git_hooks"`
+		}
+		require.NoError(t, json.Unmarshal(statusOut, &status))
+		require.Equal(t, "ready", status.CheckpointSyncState)
+		require.Equal(t, "lefthook", status.GitHooks.Mode)
+		require.Equal(t, "current", status.GitHooks.State)
+
+		s.HeadBefore = testutil.GitOutput(t, s.Dir, "rev-parse", "HEAD")
+		s.CheckpointBefore = testutil.CheckpointState(s.Dir)
+		_, err = s.RunPrompt(t, ctx,
+			"create docs/lefthook-survives.md with one sentence explaining that hooks survived, then git add and commit only that file with message 'Verify Lefthook checkpoint'. Do not ask for confirmation and do not use a worktree.")
+		require.NoError(t, err)
+
+		testutil.AssertFileExists(t, s.Dir, "docs/lefthook-survives.md")
+		testutil.AssertNewCommits(t, s, 1)
+		testutil.WaitForCheckpoint(t, s, 30*time.Second)
+		testutil.AssertCheckpointAdvanced(t, s)
+		checkpointID := testutil.AssertHasCheckpointTrailer(t, s.Dir, "HEAD")
+		testutil.AssertCheckpointExists(t, s.Dir, checkpointID)
+		testutil.WaitForNoShadowBranches(t, s.Dir, 10*time.Second)
+	})
+}
+
+// simulatedLefthookLauncher keeps the structure of a Lefthook v2 launcher but
+// dispatches directly to the clone-local script. That makes the test
+// deterministic and validates the same argv/stdin boundary without requiring a
+// separately installed Lefthook binary in every agent E2E environment.
+func simulatedLefthookLauncher(hook string) string {
+	return fmt.Sprintf(`#!/bin/sh
+
+if [ "$LEFTHOOK_VERBOSE" = "1" -o "$LEFTHOOK_VERBOSE" = "true" ]; then
+  set -x
+fi
+
+if [ "$LEFTHOOK" = "0" ]; then
+  exit 0
+fi
+
+call_lefthook()
+{
+  shift 2
+  bash ".lefthook-local/%s/entire.sh" "$@"
+}
+
+call_lefthook run "%s" "$@"
+`, hook, hook)
+}
*** End Patch";
text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));

fast-path trailer decision (`tryAgentCommitFastPath`,
`strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go`) used to trust only ACTIVE sessions, so
these commits shipped with no `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer at all. An IDLE
session with a fresh task record (`idleWithTaskContent`: in-flight or
completed-unmaterialized, each record bounded by its `StartedAt` age against
`activeSessionInteractionThreshold`, 24h) is now linkable too, so a subagent
that dies without a completion signal doesn't leave the session trusted
forever. The same predicate feeds `shouldCondenseWithOverlapCheck`'s
overlap-check bypass, so the trigger and the condensation trust share one
rule. The trailer's content guarantee is the materializer itself: the
commit's condensation stores each record's transcript-so-far under the
checkpoint's `tasks/` subtree, so no separate commit-time capture is needed.
Ordinary idle commits with no task records are unaffected — they stay exactly
as before.

### Committed Checkpoints

Branch: `entire/checkpoints/v1`

Committed checkpoints sync to exactly one git remote — the elected checkpoint
sync remote, resolved in this order:

1. `strategy_options.checkpoint_push_remote` if set — fail-closed when it
   names a remote that is not configured (checkpoint sync is disabled until
   fixed, since this is explicit user intent).
2. The **captured** election, if its remote is still configured — fail-soft
   otherwise (capture is automatic state, so a renamed/removed remote falls
   through instead of disabling sync).
3. `origin`, if configured.
4. The sole configured remote.
5. The first remote in `.git/config` order.

**Capture** is how the election follows the user's actual push habit with
zero configuration: during pre-push, when the push target agrees with the
branch's declared push destination (`branch.<name>.pushRemote` →
`remote.pushDefault` → `branch.<name>.remote` — the config a bare `git push`
resolves through) and differs from the current election, that remote is
persisted as the captured election (git common dir,
`entire-checkpoint-sync-remotes.json`, list-shaped for the future multi-remote
set), a one-line stderr notice announces the change, and the same push carries
the checkpoints. Declaration alone never elects (the config-at-rest bug that
got the static tracking tier dropped in `74e239a9` — it turned pushes to every
other remote into silent no-ops, e.g. `git clone -o base` pushing a separately
added `origin`); a bare push to an undeclared remote never elects either (the
pre-single-remote transcript leak). Phase-1 rules: at most one captured
remote, and the first still-configured capture sticks — a mixed-habit repo whose branches push
two remotes must not flip the election per push. An explicit
`checkpoint_push_remote` always outranks and disables capture. See
`strategy/checkpoint_sync_capture.go`.

For the fork setup where `origin` is an unpushable base repo, capture elects
the fork automatically on the first tracked push; `checkpoint_push_remote`
remains the explicit override.

The pre-push hook carries checkpoint data only when the push targets the
elected remote; pushes to any other remote or to a raw URL sync nothing, on
both the git-branch and git-refs backends (git-refs leaves its push queue
intact for the next elected-remote push). The dedicated `checkpoint_remote`
URL mode is exempt — it addresses a separate metadata store directly. `entire
status` shows the sync destination and how many checkpoints have not reached
it yet.

A gated push is not fully silent: when checkpoints are waiting for the
elected remote, the hook prints a two-line stderr hint naming the elected
destination, the waiting count, and the `checkpoint_push_remote` setting
(pointed at `.entire/settings.local.json` — a remote name is a per-clone
fact) that re-routes sync to the remote being pushed. The hint stays quiet
when the election was explicit (`checkpoint_push_remote` is already set),
when the push target is a raw URL rather than a configured remote, when
nothing is waiting, when the election failed (the fail-closed case logs a
warning instead), and when the push target is not the branch's declared push
destination — a deploy target or a one-off `git push upstream` must never be
recommended as the checkpoint sync remote, which would publish transcripts
there. With capture taking a declared destination on the first agreeing push,
what remains for the hint is a declared remote capture will not elect because
one is already in force (phase-1 first-capture-sticks), where naming the
setting is genuinely the only way to re-route. See `hintGatedCheckpointSync` in
`strategy/checkpoint_sync_remote.go`.

**Reads follow the election.** Where writes confine to one remote, reads
consult an ordered candidate chain: the elected sync remote first, then
`origin` as a **read-only legacy tier** — every pre-election repo has its
checkpoint data on origin, and a fresh clone may lack the local settings that
elected something else. `strategy.CheckpointReadRemotes` (and
`CheckpointReadRemotesWithElection`, which bundles the election result for
callers that need both) resolves the chain, failing *open* to `[origin]` when
the election fails — failing reads closed would only prevent *finding* data.
Every checkpoint-data read iterates the chain per operation (metadata-branch
fetches, tracking-ref readers, per-checkpoint ref fetches, blob hydration,
checkpoint-policy reads). Metadata-branch fetches refresh every candidate's
tracking ref because branch existence alone does not prove that branch contains
the requested checkpoint; they succeed when any candidate fetch succeeds.
Other reads try candidates in order, advancing on missing data or transport
failure and surfacing the first candidate's error when all fail. Local-ref advancement stays
**elected-remote-only** — `EnsurePrimaryRef`, the metadata-fetch advance step,
`promoteRemoteTrackingPrimary`, and the local checkpoint-policy ref update
never act on the legacy tier, keyed on the explicit election result rather
than the chain's first entry (a stale origin feeding `SafelyAdvanceLocalRef`
would replay local v1 onto stale history — the issue-#1374 hazard). Legacy
data on origin is therefore served through origin's *tracking ref* (resume's
final metadata tier and the store's tracking-ref fallback), never by moving
local refs. A repository with no remotes keeps its "checkpoint absent"
classification, which requires positive evidence on every axis (a successful
empty `git remote` listing, a live context, readable settings without a
`checkpoint_remote` key).

Metadata only, sharded by checkpoint ID. Supports **multiple sessions per checkpoint**:

```
<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/
├── metadata.json        # CheckpointSummary (aggregated stats)
├── 0/                   # First session (0-based indexing)
│   ├── metadata.json    # Session-specific Metadata
│   ├── full.jsonl       # Agent transcript, sanitized + redacted (CLI resume/explain)
│   ├── transcript.jsonl # Full compacted session (slice at compact_transcript_start)
│   ├── prompt.txt       # Checkpoint-scoped user prompts
│   └── content_hash.txt # sha256 of full.jsonl (dedup short-circuit)
├── 1/                   # Second session
│   ├── metadata.json
│   ├── full.jsonl
│   └── ...
├── 2/                   # Third session...
└── tasks/<tool-use-id>/ # Subagent task records, materialized at condensation
    ├── agent-<agent-id>.jsonl # Subagent transcript, sanitized + redacted (omitted when unavailable)
    └── task.json        # Record metadata (files, tokens, timings, unavailable reason); description redacted at write
```

**Compact transcript (`transcript.jsonl`):** generated best-effort from
`full.jsonl` via `transcript/compact` on every committed write and on
transcript replacement during finalization. Like `full.jsonl`, it stores the
**full compacted session** on every checkpoint (via `compact.FullWithBoundary`),
### Fixed

- Secret redaction hardened across all checkpoint persistence paths ([#395](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/395))
- Gemini session restore following latest Gemini pattern ([#403](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/403))
- Transcript path stored in checkpoint metadata breaking location independence ([#403](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/403))
- Integration tests hanging on machines with a TTY ([#414](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/414))
- Stale ACTIVE/IDLE/ENDED sessions incorrectly condensed into every commit ([#418](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/418))
- Gemini TTY handling when called as a hook ([#430](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/430))
- Deselected agents reappearing as pre-selected on re-enable ([#443](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/443))
- UTF-8 truncation producing garbled text for CJK/emoji characters ([#444](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/444))
- Git refs resembling CLI flags causing errors ([#446](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/446))
- Over-aggressive secret redaction in session transcripts ([#471](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/471))

### Docs

- Security and privacy documentation ([#398](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/398))
- Agent integration checklist for validating new agent integrations ([#442](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/442))
- Clarified README wording and agent-agnostic troubleshooting ([#453](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/453))

### Thanks

Thanks to @AlienKevin for contributing to this release!

Thanks to @ammarateya ([#220](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/220)), @Avyukth ([#257](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/257)), and @MementoMori123 ([#315](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/315)) for their OpenCode PRs! We've now merged our OpenCode integration. While we went with our own implementation, your PRs were valuable in helping us validate our design choices and ensure we covered the right scenarios. We appreciate the effort you put into this!

## [0.4.5] - 2026-02-17

### Added

- Detect external hook managers (Husky, Lefthook, Overcommit) and warn during `entire enable` ([#373](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/373))
- New E2E test workflow running on merge to main ([#350](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/350), [#351](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/351))
- Subagent file modifications are now properly detected ([#323](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/323))
- Content-aware carry-forward for 1:1 checkpoint-to-commit mapping ([#325](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/325))

### Changed

- Consolidated duplicate JSONL transcript parsers into a shared `transcript` package ([#346](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/346))
- Replaced `ApplyCommonActions` with `ActionHandler` interface for cleaner hook dispatch ([#332](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/332))

### Fixed

- Extra shadow branches accumulating when agent commits some files and user commits the rest ([#367](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/367))
- Attribution calculation for worktree inflation and mid-turn agent commits ([#366](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/366))
- All IDLE sessions being incorrectly added to a checkpoint ([#359](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/359))
- Hook directory resolution now uses `git --git-path hooks` for correctness ([#355](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/355))
- Gemini transcript parsing: array content format and trailer blank line separation for single-line commits ([#342](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/342))

### Docs

- Added concurrent ACTIVE sessions limitation to contributing guide ([#326](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/326))

```
    ├── agent-<agent-id>.jsonl # Subagent transcript, sanitized + redacted (omitted when unavailable)
    └── task.json        # Record metadata (files, tokens, timings, unavailable reason); description redacted at write
```

**Compact transcript (`transcript.jsonl`):** generated best-effort from
`full.jsonl` via `transcript/compact` on every committed write and on
transcript replacement during finalization. Like `full.jsonl`, it stores the
**full compacted session** on every checkpoint (via `compact.FullWithBoundary`),
### Fixed

- Secret redaction hardened across all checkpoint persistence paths ([#395](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/395))

### Docs

Thanks to @AlienKevin for contributing to this release!

Thanks to @ammarateya ([#220](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/220)), @Avyukth ([#257](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/257)), and @MementoMori123 ([#315](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/315)) for their OpenCode PRs! We've now merged our OpenCode integration. While we went with our own implementation, your PRs were valuable in helping us validate our design choices and ensure we covered the right scenarios. We appreciate the effort you put into this!
